title: Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid-Base Imbalances
introduction: Water and electrolytes maintain physiological homeostasis across intracellular and extracellular compartments, enabling proper organ function and survival[cite: 399, 400]. Understanding fluid distribution mechanisms, intravenous solution pharmacology, acid-base regulation, and sodium, potassium, and calcium imbalances equips nurses to detect early clinical deterioration and deliver safe, targeted interventions[cite: 403, 405, 407, 415, 417, 420].
learningOutcomes: 6.1 Describe the distribution of body water across intracellular (ICF) and extracellular (ECF) compartments, calculate fluid weight equivalents, and distinguish electrolytes from non-electrolytes[cite: 399, 400, 401].
6.2 Differentiate osmolality from osmolarity, explain isotonic, hypertonic, and hypotonic fluid shifts, and compare crystalloid versus colloid intravenous solutions[cite: 402, 403, 404].
6.3 Explain the four mechanisms of fluid distribution, normal routes of daily fluid loss, and the clinical and nursing management of ECF volume deficit and excess[cite: 405, 406, 409, 410, 411].
6.4 Outline the renal, respiratory, and chemical buffer systems regulating acid-base balance and differentiate acidosis from respiratory and metabolic alkalosis[cite: 407, 408, 411, 413, 414].
6.5 Analyze the causes, clinical manifestations, laboratory thresholds, and nursing/medical management of sodium, potassium, and calcium imbalances[cite: 415, 416, 417, 418, 419, 420, 421].

content.heading: Dynamics of Body Fluids, Electrolytes, and Osmolality
content.body: Body fluids consist of water and electrolytes, with water making up roughly 60% of adult body weight—varying by age, gender, and body fat (adipose tissue contains only 20% water)[cite: 399]. Infants have 70–80% body water, young adult males have 60% (more skeletal muscle), young adult females have 50% (more body fat), and older adults decline to 45–55%, making infants and the elderly most vulnerable to fluid disorders[cite: 399]. Fluid resides in two major compartments: Intracellular Fluid (ICF), which holds two-thirds of body water (24 L of 40 L; 40% of body weight), and Extracellular Fluid (ECF), which holds one-third (20% of body weight—roughly 11 L in a 70 kg man, split into 3 L plasma, 8 L interstitial fluid, and 1 L in specialized cavities like lymph, CSF, eye humors, synovial, and serous fluids)[cite: 400, 401]. Trapping of ECF in spaces unavailable for ICF-ECF exchange is termed a third-space fluid shift[cite: 401]. Clinically, 1,000 mL (1 L) of fluid equals 1 kg (2.2 lbs), making sudden weight changes a sensitive measure of fluid balance[cite: 401]. Electrolytes ionize in water into positive cations (potassium, sodium, magnesium) and negative anions (chloride, bicarbonate): potassium (K+) and phosphate (HPO4) predominate in ICF, whereas sodium (Na+) and chloride (Cl-) predominate in ECF, with sodium primarily determining ECF concentration[cite: 401]. Non-electrolytes (glucose, proteins, O2, CO2, organic acids) carry no electrical charge in water[cite: 401]. Osmolality (mOsm/kg of water; normal 275–295 mOsm/kg, determined chiefly by glucose and sodium) describes internal body fluids like plasma and urine, whereas osmolarity (mOsm/L of total volume) describes external solutions[cite: 402, 403]. Values above 295 mOsm/kg indicate fluid volume deficit[cite: 403]. Water shifts toward whichever compartment has higher osmolality: isotonic solutions (0.9% saline) leave cell volume unchanged, hypertonic solutions (>0.9% saline) draw water out and shrink cells, and hypotonic solutions (e.g., 0.2% saline) move water in and swell cells[cite: 403].

content.heading: IV Fluids (Crystalloids vs. Colloids), Fluid Distribution, and Normal Losses
content.body: Intravenous solutions fall into two categories: crystalloids and colloids[cite: 403]. Crystalloids contain small, easily dissolved electrolyte or non-electrolyte (e.g., dextrose) molecules that cross semipermeable membranes freely, expanding both intravascular and interstitial spaces and categorized by pre-infusion tonicity relative to plasma[cite: 403, 404]. Colloids (albumin, dextrans, hydroxyethyl starches)—also called plasma or volume expanders—contain molecules too large to cross capillary walls; they remain intravascular, exert high oncotic pressure to draw interstitial fluid into vessels, require less total volume, and act for several days when capillary walls are intact, making them ideal for hypoproteinemia, malnutrition, or patients who cannot tolerate large fluid volumes[cite: 403, 404]. Fluid and solutes move across body compartments via four mechanisms: osmosis (fluid moving from lower to higher solute concentration across a membrane), diffusion (solute/fluid movement from higher to lower concentration), filtration (fluid and particles moving across a partial barrier, such as from arterial capillaries to interstitial fluid), and active transport (energy-requiring movement of ions against a concentration gradient, such as the sodium-potassium pump)[cite: 405, 406]. Normal daily fluid losses occur through the kidneys (1–2 L/day), skin evaporation (500–600 mL/day, rising with fever), lungs via exhaled water vapor (500 mL/day, rising with fever), and the GI tract (100–200 mL/day)[cite: 406]. Bedside deficit assessment monitors intake/output, urine specific gravity, skin turgor (sternum, inner thigh, forehead), daily weights, sticky saliva/thirst, neck vein distension at 45° elevation (positive in fluid overload or heart failure), mental status, rapid weak pulse, and dependent hand vein filling time (normal 3–5 seconds; >5 seconds indicates dehydration)[cite: 406].

content.heading: Extracellular Fluid Volume Deficit (FVD) and Excess (FVE)
content.body: Extracellular Fluid Volume Deficit (FVD) results from proportional water-electrolyte losses (vomiting, diarrhea, fever, fistulae), reduced intake (dysphagia, coma, tube feeding), or third-spacing (bowel obstruction, burns, cavity effusions)[cite: 409]. Clinical signs include longitudinal tongue furrows, decreased skin turgor, urine output below 30 mL/hr, slow hand vein filling, flat supine neck veins, weight loss (2% mild, 5% moderate, 8% severe), orthostatic systolic blood pressure drop of 10 mmHg or more, low CVP, subnormal temperature (unless infected), compensatory tachycardia/tachypnea, and elevated hemoglobin, hematocrit, and urine specific gravity[cite: 409]. Untreated FVD risks acute renal tubular deterioration, bicarbonate and potassium deficits, and hypovolemic shock[cite: 409]. Nursing care includes adding supplementary water to tube feeds, avoiding oral water during nasogastric suction (offer occasional ice chips instead to prevent electrolyte depletion), irrigating NG tubes strictly with isotonic solution rather than water, monitoring vital signs/CVP/breath sounds to prevent overload, frequent oral care, and advising slow position changes[cite: 409]. Conversely, Extracellular Fluid Volume Excess (FVE) arises from sodium and water retention in chronic heart failure, chronic renal failure, or excessive sodium-containing IV infusions[cite: 410]. Signs include puffy eyelids, pitting peripheral edema (1+ to 4+, cool skin), ascites, third-space effusions, moist lung rales (signaling ≥1,500 mL excess), full bounding pulse, elevated CVP, slow hand vein emptying when raised, distended neck veins, and hemodilution (decreased hemoglobin and hematocrit), risking pulmonary edema[cite: 410, 411]. Management combines sodium-restricted diets with diuretics—thiazides, loop diuretics (furosemide/Lasix acting on the ascending Loop of Henle, requiring potassium supplements), or potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone/Aldactone, triamterene/Dyrenium inhibiting aldosterone, risking hyperkalemia)—plus daily same-time weights, strict I&O, high Fowler's positioning, bed rest to promote diuresis, abdominal girth measurement, and skin/turning care[cite: 410, 411].

content.heading: Acid-Base Regulation, Acidosis, and Alkalosis
content.body: Acids ionize in water to donate hydrogen ions (H+), whereas bases accept hydrogen ions; normal arterial plasma pH is tightly maintained near 7.4 (7.35–7.45)[cite: 405]. Metabolic acid sources include CO2 from glucose breakdown, fatty/keto acids from fat metabolism, sulphuric acid from protein metabolism, lactic acid from anaerobic glycolysis, and intracellular acid release from cell destruction, while bases enter via oral/IV bicarbonates, citrate from blood transfusions, and TPN[cite: 408, 409]. Three homeostatic systems preserve pH: (1) Chemical buffers (carbonic acid-bicarbonate maintaining a 20:1 bicarbonate-to-carbonic-acid ratio, phosphate, plasma/intracellular proteins, and hemoglobin); (2) Respiratory system (eliminating CO2/H2CO3, driven primarily by PaCO2); and (3) Renal system (conserving filtered HCO3- and excreting excess H+ as free H+, ammonium NH4+, or weak acids)[cite: 407, 408]. Acidosis (arterial pH <7.35, with CO2 >45 mmHg in respiratory causes) stems from acid overproduction or under-elimination, disturbing K+, Ca2+, and Na+ levels in high-risk patients with respiratory depression, COPD, ARDS, pneumonia, chest trauma, pneumothorax, poisoning, or obesity[cite: 411, 412]. Nursing interventions target patent airways, hourly respiratory monitoring, ABG and daily electrolyte checks, pulmonary physiotherapy, oxygen, bronchodilators (salbutamol, aminophylline, atropine, ephedrine), and mucolytics (acetylcysteine)[cite: 412, 413]. Alkalosis (excess bicarbonate or depleted carbonic acid, pH >7.45) presents as Respiratory Alkalosis (hyperventilation losing CO2 in anxiety, fever, ventilator missettings, CNS lesions, aspirin, or epinephrine; CO2 <35 mmHg, HCO3- <22 mEq/L) or Metabolic Alkalosis (bicarbonate gain or acid loss via prolonged vomiting, NG suction, Cushing's syndrome, hyperaldosteronism, thiazides, or excess Lactated Ringer's; HCO3- >29 mEq/L)[cite: 413, 414]. Manifestations include tachycardia, hypotension, hypokalemia (increasing digoxin toxicity >2.4 ng/mL), agitation, perioral/toe paresthesias, seizures, hyperreflexia, muscle cramps, and tetany with hypocalcemia (<8.5 mg/dL, positive Chvostek-Weiss and Trousseau's signs)[cite: 414, 415].

content.heading: Sodium and Potassium Imbalances
content.body: Sodium regulates ECF volume, osmotic equilibrium, blood volume, nerve conduction, and cardiac contractility, with renal sodium reabsorption retaining chloride and water[cite: 415]. Hyponatremia (plasma Na+ <135 mEq/L; urine specific gravity <1.010) stems from sodium loss or water excess (low-Na diet, GI fluid loss, loop diuretics, CHF, sodium-free IV fluids, water intoxication, unacclimatized heat exhaustion)[cite: 415, 416]. It causes lethargy, headache, confusion, seizures, coma, weakness, diminished reflexes, nausea/vomiting/anorexia, and hyperactive bowel sounds (plus hypertension and high CVP if hypervolemic), managed by water restriction, oral/IV sodium replacement, or osmotic diuretics like mannitol in hypervolemic cases[cite: 416]. Hypernatremia (plasma Na+ >145 mEq/L; osmolality >300 mOsm/kg; urine specific gravity >1.030 in non-renal water loss) results from poor water intake, high-protein tube feeds without water, hyperglycemia, diabetes insipidus (low ADH), or excess hypertonic saline[cite: 416, 417]. Signs include intense thirst, rough dry red tongue, flushed skin, low-grade fever, firm rubbery turgor, restlessness, mania, convulsions, and oliguria/anuria, treated with sodium-free hypotonic IV fluids (5% dextrose, hypotonic saline), oral water, diuretics, and dietary sodium restriction[cite: 416, 417]. Potassium is the primary ICF cation—essential for cellular healing and growth, nerve conduction, and cardiac/skeletal muscle function—with kidneys excreting 90–95%[cite: 417, 418]. Hypokalemia (serum K+ <3.5 mEq/L from potassium-losing diuretics, GI losses, poor intake, or hyperaldosteronism) causes hyperpolarization, paralytic ileus, shallow respirations, postural hypotension, polyuria/nocturia, decreased reflexes, digitalis sensitivity, and classic ECG changes (ST depression, inverted T waves, prominent peaked U wave, fatal ventricular dysrhythmias)[cite: 418, 419]. Hyperkalemia (repeated plasma K+ >5.6 mEq/L from renal failure, burns/crush injuries releasing cellular K+, adrenal insufficiency, or excess K+-sparing diuretics) progresses from anxiety, cramps, and diarrhea (~5.3 mEq/L) to paresthesia (6 mEq/L), bradycardia (7 mEq/L), heart block (9 mEq/L), and fatal cardiac standstill (>8.5 mEq/L), showing tall narrow T waves and widened QRS complexes on ECG[cite: 419]. Emergency hyperkalemia management uses IV calcium (to rapidly antagonize cardiac toxicity), insulin with hypertonic dextrose, and IV sodium bicarbonate (both shifting K+ back into cells)[cite: 419].

content.heading: Calcium Imbalances: Hypocalcemia and Hypercalcemia
content.body: Calcium is regulated by parathyroid hormone (PTH), calcitonin, and Vitamin D, and serves six essential functions: decreasing neuromuscular irritability (increasing stability), reducing capillary permeability, promoting muscle contractility, aiding nerve conduction, enabling blood clotting, and building bones and teeth[cite: 420, 421]. Hypocalcemia (plasma Ca2+ <9 mg/dL or 2.25 mmol/L) arises from PTH deficiency, Vitamin D deficiency, renal failure, low magnesium (which suppresses PTH secretion), pancreatitis, alcoholism, diarrhea, intestinal fluid loss, or aggressive diuretics[cite: 420, 421]. Clinical manifestations reflect heightened neuromuscular excitability: perioral and extremity paresthesias, hyperactive reflexes, skeletal muscle cramps and tetany, life-threatening laryngospasm (stridor), convulsions, heart block or ventricular fibrillation, brittle nails, osteoporosis/fractures, positive Trousseau's sign (carpal spasm with palmar flexion after inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure for 1–4 minutes), and positive Chvostek's sign (lip and cheek spasm upon tapping the facial nerve anterior to the ear)[cite: 415, 420]. Treatment includes IV calcium gluconate, synthetic parathormone, and oral calcium carbonate in divided doses, paired with airway monitoring for laryngospasm and seizure precautions[cite: 421]. Hypercalcemia (serum Ca2+ >10.2 mg/dL or 2.55 mmol/L) results from hyperparathyroidism, bony metastases, multiple myeloma, prolonged immobilization, Vitamin D overdose, or kidney stones[cite: 421]. Because excess calcium acts as a sedative at the myoneural junction, it produces hypotonic skeletal muscles, lethargy, stupor, coma, anorexia, constipation, nausea/vomiting, polydipsia/polyuria, dehydration, deep bony pain, flank pain, and cardiac arrest[cite: 421]. Treatment promotes renal calcium excretion via high-volume isotonic saline hydration (3,000–4,000 mL/day) and furosemide (Lasix), alongside synthetic calcitonin, low-calcium diet, mobilization, and osteoclast-inhibiting pamidronate (Aredia)[cite: 421].

inTextQuestions.question: Why should a nurse never give plain oral water or irrigate a nasogastric (NG) tube with plain water in a patient on continuous NG suction?
inTextQuestions.answer: Plain water draws electrolytes out of the gastric mucosal wall into the gastric lumen by diffusion, which are then suctioned away, worsening electrolyte depletion; NG tubes must always be irrigated with isotonic solution, and patients may occasionally suck ice chips[cite: 409].

inTextQuestions.question: What normal bicarbonate-to-carbonic-acid ratio is required by the body's primary chemical buffer system to maintain normal arterial plasma pH (~7.4)?
inTextQuestions.answer: A ratio of 20:1 (20 parts bicarbonate to 1 part carbonic acid)[cite: 405, 408].

inTextQuestions.question: Compare the hallmark ECG changes seen in hypokalemia versus early hyperkalemia.
inTextQuestions.answer: Hypokalemia produces ST-segment depression, inverted T waves, and an enlarged/peaked U wave (risking ventricular dysrhythmias), whereas early hyperkalemia produces tall, narrow T waves and a widened QRS complex[cite: 418, 419].

inTextQuestions.question: How are positive Chvostek's sign and positive Trousseau's sign elicited during a bedside assessment for hypocalcemia?
inTextQuestions.answer: Positive Chvostek's sign occurs when tapping the facial nerve on the cheek in front of the ear causes lip and cheek spasm; positive Trousseau's sign occurs when inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for 1–4 minutes (occluding the brachial artery) triggers carpal spasm with palmar flexion[cite: 415, 420].

saqs.question: Describe the distribution of body water across ICF and ECF compartments, explain why infants and older adults are at greater risk for fluid imbalance, and distinguish crystalloids from colloids.
saqs.answer: Body water averages 60% of adult body weight—two-thirds resides in ICF (40% body weight) and one-third in ECF (20% body weight, comprising plasma, interstitial fluid, and specialized cavities)[cite: 399, 400]. Infants have high body water (70–80%) while older adults drop to 45–55%, making both age groups more vulnerable to fluid disorders[cite: 399]. Crystalloids contain small solute molecules that cross semipermeable membranes to expand both intravascular and interstitial spaces, whereas colloids (albumin, dextrans, hydroxyethyl starches) contain large molecules that stay intravascular and pull interstitial fluid inward via high oncotic pressure[cite: 403, 404].

saqs.question: Compare the clinical observations, laboratory findings, and nursing care of Extracellular Fluid Volume Deficit (FVD) versus Extracellular Fluid Volume Excess (FVE).
saqs.answer: FVD presents with tongue furrows, poor skin turgor, urine output <30 mL/hr, flat supine neck veins, weight loss (2–8%), orthostatic hypotension, and elevated Hgb, Hct, and urine specific gravity—managed by careful IV fluids, isotonic NG irrigation, oral care, and slow position changes[cite: 409]. FVE presents with puffy eyelids, pitting edema (1+ to 4+), ascites, moist lung rales, bounding pulse, distended neck veins, high CVP, and decreased Hgb/Hct—managed by sodium restriction, diuretics, high Fowler's positioning, bed rest, daily weights, strict I&O, and abdominal girth monitoring[cite: 410, 411].

saqs.question: Define acidosis and alkalosis, state the three homeostatic systems that regulate acid-base balance, and differentiate respiratory alkalosis from metabolic alkalosis.
saqs.answer: Acidosis is an excess of plasma H+ causing arterial pH <7.35, whereas alkalosis reflects excess bicarbonate or decreased carbonic acid (pH >7.45)[cite: 411, 413, 414]. Acid-base balance is regulated by chemical buffers (20:1 bicarbonate-to-carbonic-acid ratio), the respiratory system (CO2 excretion), and the renal system (HCO3- conservation and H+ excretion)[cite: 407, 408]. Respiratory alkalosis results from CO2 loss via hyperventilation (CO2 <35 mmHg, HCO3- <22 mEq/L), whereas metabolic alkalosis results from bicarbonate gain or acid loss such as prolonged vomiting or NG suction (HCO3- >29 mEq/L)[cite: 413, 414].

saqs.question: Compare the laboratory thresholds, clinical signs, and emergency treatment of hypokalemia and hyperkalemia.
saqs.answer: Hypokalemia (serum K+ <3.5 mEq/L) causes paralytic ileus, shallow respirations, postural hypotension, decreased reflexes, and ST depression/inverted T/peaked U waves on ECG[cite: 418, 419]. Hyperkalemia (plasma K+ >5.6 mEq/L; >8.5 mEq/L often fatal) causes cramps, diarrhea, paresthesias, bradycardia, heart block, and tall narrow T waves with widened QRS[cite: 419]. Emergency hyperkalemia treatment includes IV calcium to antagonize cardiac toxicity immediately, plus insulin with hypertonic dextrose and IV sodium bicarbonate to shift K+ from ECF back into ICF[cite: 419].

saqs.question: List four physiological functions of calcium and contrast the causes, neuromuscular signs, and medical management of hypocalcemia versus hypercalcemia.
saqs.answer: Calcium decreases neuromuscular irritability, lowers capillary permeability, supports muscle contractility and nerve conduction, and is essential for blood clotting, bones, and teeth[cite: 420, 421]. Hypocalcemia (<9 mg/dL; caused by PTH/Vitamin D deficiency, renal failure, low Mg2+, or pancreatitis) causes tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, and positive Chvostek's/Trousseau's signs—treated with IV calcium gluconate, oral calcium carbonate, airway monitoring, and seizure precautions[cite: 420, 421]. Hypercalcemia (>10.2 mg/dL; caused by hyperparathyroidism, bony metastases, multiple myeloma, or immobilization) causes hypotonic muscles, lethargy, bone/flank pain, constipation, and coma—treated with isotonic saline (3,000–4,000 mL/day), furosemide (Lasix), calcitonin, mobilization, low-calcium diet, and pamidronate[cite: 421].
